fields.title: Grace Abounding (For Teens)
fields.description: At about twenty, John Bunyan was the worst swearer his neighbours had ever heard. A few years later he was so sure he had committed the one sin God cannot forgive that his body shook for days, and he knew “what it was to be weary of my life, and yet afraid to die.” Grace Abounding is his own story, written in a Bedford prison cell, of years of doubt, unwanted blasphemous thoughts and despair, and of a few words of the Bible that broke through. This teen edition keeps his words and his hardest honesty, and speaks plainly to anyone fighting thoughts they never wanted.
fields.hook: Sure he had committed the one sin God can’t forgive, until a few words of the Bible broke through.

qa.question: Who was John Bunyan?
qa.answer: An English tinker, a mender of pots and pans, born at Elstow near Bedford in 1628. He served as a teenage soldier in Parliament's army during the Civil War, joined a small church in Bedford in the 1650s, and became a popular preacher. He was imprisoned for twelve years, from 1660 to 1672, for preaching outside the Church of England, and later wrote The Pilgrim's Progress. He died in 1688.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It keeps his swearing and his years as a “painted hypocrite,” a year of blasphemous thoughts he could not stop, his terror that he had committed the unpardonable sin, and the time he was “weary of my life, and yet afraid to die.” It also keeps what his imprisonment cost his wife and children, especially his blind daughter.

qa.question: What does “My grace is sufficient for thee” mean in his story?
qa.answer: It is a line from 2 Corinthians 12:9. At first only the words “My grace is sufficient” came to him, and he longed for the words “for thee.” Later, in a church meeting, he heard the whole phrase three times over, and it felt as if Jesus were speaking it to him personally. It became one of the turning points of his recovery.

qa.question: Did Bunyan really hear voices from heaven?
qa.answer: He describes words that seemed to “dart” into his soul, such as the question during a game of cat, “Wilt thou leave thy sins and go to heaven, or have thy sins and go to hell?” He reports them as he experienced them. He was also careful: of one strange experience, a rushing wind and a voice, he wrote that he did not rest his salvation on it but “upon the Lord Jesus, in the promise.”

qa.question: Did Bunyan commit the unpardonable sin?
qa.answer: He feared for over two years that he had, after the thought “Let Him go, if He will” passed through his exhausted mind. But when he finally read the frightening passages in Hebrews carefully, he saw they describe a complete, open turning away from Christ, not a thought he hated and fought. He concluded his fears came from being “misinformed of the nature of my sin.” Many people today have unwanted thoughts like his; they are common, they are not who you are, and a pastor together with a doctor or counsellor can help.

qa.question: How did he treat other people?
qa.answer: He tried to win his old friends away from their ways, and he grieved more over converts who fell away than he would over the death of one of his own children. When he was slandered he refused to hit back, and he prayed for his accusers that God would give them repentance. In prison his deepest worry was for his family, and above all his blind daughter.

qa.question: What is the original book, and when and why was it written?
qa.answer: Its full title is Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners. Bunyan wrote it in 1666 while he was in Bedford gaol, for the people who had come to faith through his preaching, so that they and others would remember how God had worked in his soul. He said he would tell it “plain and simple” and “lay down the thing as it was.”

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from it?
qa.answer: That doubts, fears and even horrible unwanted thoughts are more common than you think and do not mean God has given up on you; that you should tell someone safe rather than fight alone; and that your standing with God rests on Christ, not on your feelings. As Bunyan put it, his righteousness was “Jesus Christ Himself, the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever.”

fields.title: Few Equals
fields.body_html:
“This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15 (KJV)

John Bunyan was born in 1628 in Elstow, a village near Bedford in the middle of England. His father mended pots and pans for a living, and Bunyan never pretended his family was anything special: “my father's house being of that rank that is meanest and most despised of all the families in the land.” His parents sent him to school long enough to learn to read and write, and then, he admits, “I did soon lose that little I learned.”

He wrote this book in 1666, from a prison cell in Bedford, for the people who had come to faith through his preaching. He called it Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, and it is one of the most honest books any Christian has written about the inside of his own head. He promised to tell it straight, with no fancy style: “God did not play in convincing of me, the devil did not play in tempting of me, neither did I play when I sunk as into a bottomless pit.” So, he said, he would “be plain and simple, and lay down the thing as it was.”

As a boy, by his own account, he was a champion swearer. He had “but few equals, especially considering my years, which were tender, being few, both for cursing, swearing, lying, and blaspheming the holy name of God.” And yet at nine or ten he was having nightmares about devils trying to drag him away, and lying awake terrified of the day of judgment. He was so scared of hell that he wished “either that there had been no hell, or that I had been a devil,” because then at least he would be the one doing the tormenting. That is a strange, dark thought for a ten-year-old. He told it anyway.

The nightmares faded, and so did the fear. “My pleasures did quickly cut off the remembrance of them, as if they had never been.” By his late teens he was “the very ringleader of all the youth that kept me company, into all manner of vice and ungodliness.” He couldn't stand religion. Watching someone read a Christian book felt to him “as it were a prison.”

Still, something in him expected more of believers than he expected of himself. Once, when he heard a man known as religious swear an oath, “it had so great a stroke upon my spirit, that it made my heart to ache.”

Several times he nearly died. He fell into a creek of the sea and “hardly escaped drowning.” He fell out of a boat into the river at Bedford. He stunned an adder with a stick, forced its mouth open, and pulled out what he took to be its sting with his fingers. As a teenage soldier in Parliament's army during the English Civil War, he was picked to go to a siege, but another man asked to go in his place. “Coming to the siege, as he stood sentinel, he was shot into the head with a musket bullet, and died.”

Bunyan's verdict on all of it is short: “Here, as I said, were judgments and mercy, but neither of them did awaken my soul to righteousness.” Close calls don't change a heart on their own. Plenty of people walk away from a crash or a scare and go straight back to how they were. He did.

Notice two things about how this book begins. First, Bunyan does not make himself look good. He is writing to people who look up to him, and he opens with his swearing and his nightmares. Second, the fear he felt as a child did not make him good. Fear can make you miserable without making you different. What finally changes Bunyan is not terror but grace, and this whole book is the story of how long it took him to believe that grace was for him.

One thing to do this week: think of a close call or a real scare in your own life. Write down one sentence about it, and then answer honestly: did it change anything in me, or did I go straight back? There's no wrong answer. Bunyan's honesty starts with exactly that kind of question.

study_questions.question: What kind of family did John Bunyan come from?
study_questions.answer: A poor one. His father mended pots and pans, and Bunyan called his father's house the “meanest and most despised” rank in the land.

study_questions.question: Why does Bunyan say he will write “plain and simple”?
study_questions.answer: Because God, the devil and his own suffering were all deadly serious, so he would not “play” in telling it but would “lay down the thing as it was.”

study_questions.question: Did his near escapes from death change him?
study_questions.answer: No. He says they were “judgments and mercy,” but neither of them woke his soul up, and he went on sinning.

fields.title: Wilt Thou Leave Thy Sins?
fields.body_html:
“Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.” — Isaiah 55:7 (KJV)

At about twenty Bunyan married. He doesn't tell us his wife's name, and nobody now knows it for certain. They were so poor they didn't have “so much household stuff as a dish or spoon betwixt us both.” But she brought two Christian books her father had left her, The Plain Man's Pathway to Heaven and The Practice of Piety, and the two of them sometimes read them together. She often told him what a godly man her father had been.

It didn't reach his heart, but it gave him a taste for religion of the respectable kind. He went to church twice a day, “and that too with the foremost,” and sang and prayed with great devotion, “yet retaining my wicked life.” He was so impressed by the church building, the priest and the robes that he could have lain down and let the priest walk on him. He even asked his father whether their family might be descended from the Israelites, God's chosen people, hoping that would make him safe. His father said no.

Then one Sunday the parson preached about keeping the Sabbath, and about the wrong of spending it on sport. Sunday was exactly when Bunyan did his worst. He went home “with a great burden upon my spirit,” feeling, for the first time he could remember, what guilt was. It lasted until about lunchtime. “But oh! how glad was I, that this trouble was gone from me, and that the fire was put out, that I might sin again without control!”

That same afternoon he was playing a game called cat, a bit like a mix of cricket and rounders, where you hit a small piece of wood with a stick. He had just hit it once and was about to hit it again when, he says, “a voice did suddenly dart from heaven into my soul, which said, 'Wilt thou leave thy sins and go to heaven, or have thy sins and go to hell?'” He dropped the stick and looked up, and it seemed to him that he saw Jesus looking down at him, very displeased.

You would expect that to be the turning point. It wasn't. Straight away a different thought fastened on him: it was too late. Christ would never forgive someone like him. And if he was going to be lost anyway, why stop? “I can but be damned, and if I must be so, I had as good be damned for many sins, as to be damned for few.” So he went back to the game and told nobody. For about a month after that he threw himself into sin as fast as he could, “lest I should die before I had my desire.”

Bunyan was sure this kind of hopelessness is far more common than people realise. He calls it a temptation that is “more than usual amongst poor creatures than many are aware of”: a quiet, settled feeling that there is no hope for you, so you may as well keep going the wrong way.

That is worth stopping on. “It's too late for me, so why bother?” sounds like being realistic. It's not. It is despair pretending to be honesty, and it always pushes you further into the very thing you wish you could leave. If you have ever thought, “I've already blown it, so I might as well keep going,” you have heard the same lie Bunyan heard on that Sunday afternoon. The voice he heard asked him a real question, and a question means a door is still open.

One thing to do this week: next time you catch yourself thinking “I've already ruined it, so what's the point,” stop and do one small right thing anyway: switch it off, walk away, send the apology. You don't have to fix everything. You just have to refuse the lie that it's too late.

study_questions.answer: He seemed to hear a voice asking whether he would leave his sins and go to heaven or keep them and go to hell, and he looked up as if Jesus were looking down at him, displeased.

study_questions.question: Why did he go back to sinning straight afterwards?
study_questions.answer: He decided it was too late for him to be forgiven, so he might as well “be damned for many sins” as for few. It was despair, not honesty.

fields.title: A Poor Painted Hypocrite
fields.body_html:
“for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.” — 1 Samuel 16:7 (KJV)

One day Bunyan was standing at a neighbour's shop window, “cursing and swearing, and playing the madman, after my wonted manner.” The woman of the house heard him. She was no saint herself, but she told him he was “the ungodliest fellow for swearing that ever she heard in all her life,” and that he was “able to spoil all the youth in a whole town, if they came but in my company.”

It went straight in. He stood there with his head down and wished “that I might be a little child again, that my father might learn me to speak without this wicked way of swearing.” He was sure he could never change. And then, to his own amazement, he did. “How it came to pass, I know not.” He just stopped swearing, and found he could speak “better, and with more pleasantness, than ever I could before.”

Around then he got to know a poor man who talked about the Bible in a way he liked. Bunyan started reading it himself, mostly the stories. He cleaned up his life, set the Ten Commandments in front of him as his way to heaven, and when he broke one he said sorry and promised God to do better. He thought, he says, “I pleased God as well as any man in England.”

The neighbours could not believe it. One minute he was the worst swearer in the village, the next he was a model of good behaviour. He compares it to a man from Bedlam, London's hospital for the mentally ill, suddenly becoming sober. People praised him to his face and behind his back, and he loved it. “For though, as yet, I was nothing but a poor painted hypocrite, yet I loved to be talked of as one that was truly godly.” He kept this up for about a year.

There is a strange little story from this time. Bunyan loved bell-ringing, but decided it was a vanity and gave it up. Yet he couldn't stay away, so he went to watch the others ring. Then he began to think: what if a bell fell? He stood under a big beam. But what if a bell swung, hit the wall and bounced onto him? He moved to the door. Then: “How, if the steeple itself should fall?” The thought shook him so much that in the end he ran away from the church altogether. Giving up dancing, he says, took him a whole year.

Looking back, his judgement on that year is blunt: he was “all this while ignorant of Jesus Christ, and going about to establish my own righteousness.” He had changed his behaviour and his reputation, but he still didn't know Christ at all.

Two things here are worth taking home. First, it is possible to get really good at looking Christian, and to enjoy the praise, while your heart hasn't met God. Bunyan's word for it is “painted,” like a face with make-up on. A phone full of filtered photos makes this easier than it has ever been. Second, notice that steeple. Bunyan had a mind that ran “what if” chains, each one scarier than the last. Lots of people do. If yours does too, you are not strange, and you are not alone. We will come back to that, because it matters for what happens to him next.

One thing to do this week: do one genuinely good thing this week that nobody sees, and don't mention it to anyone or post about it. Notice whether keeping quiet about it is easy or hard. That tells you something about who you are doing it for.

study_questions.question: What made Bunyan stop swearing?
study_questions.answer: A woman who was far from godly herself told him he swore worse than anyone she had ever heard and could spoil all the young people in the town. He was ashamed, and found to his surprise that he stopped.

study_questions.question: Why does he call himself a “poor painted hypocrite”?
study_questions.answer: Because his outward life had changed and he loved being praised as godly, but he still did not know Christ and was trying to make himself right with God by his own efforts.

study_questions.question: What does the bell-ringing story show about Bunyan's mind?
study_questions.answer: That it ran in anxious “what if” chains, from a falling bell to a falling steeple, until fear drove him away altogether.

fields.title: Women in the Sun
fields.body_html:
“Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.” — Matthew 7:14 (KJV)

Bunyan worked as a tinker too, walking from village to village mending things. One day his work took him to Bedford, and in one of the streets he came across “three or four poor women sitting at a door in the sun, and talking about the things of God.” By now he thought of himself as a bit of an expert on religion, so he drew near to listen. “I heard, but I understood not.”

They weren't talking about rules. “Their talk was about a new birth, the work of God on their hearts.” They talked about how God had shown them his love in Jesus, about the promises that had comforted them, and about their own unbelief and how useless their own goodness was. And they talked like happy people: “methought they spake as if joy did make them speak.” To Bunyan it was as if they had found a new world.

His heart began to shake. He realised he had never once thought about a new birth. He went back to his work, but their conversation went with him, and he kept finding excuses to go back and listen again. He noticed two new things inside himself: a soft, tender heart, and a mind that wouldn't stop thinking about God. His mind, he says, hung on to it “like a horse leech at the vein.”

Not everyone he knew was going the same way. He had a close friend named Harry, a hard swearer, whom he now stopped spending time with. When they met in a lane and Bunyan asked him why he swore like that and what would happen to him if he died, Harry snapped back, “What would the devil do for company, if it were not for such as I am?” The poor man who had first got Bunyan reading the Bible joined a group called the Ranters, who taught that people who had reached their kind of perfection couldn't sin whatever they did. Bunyan, unsure what was true, prayed one of the most sensible prayers in the book: “O Lord, I am a fool, and not able to know the truth from error: Lord, leave me not to my own blindness.”

But his anxious mind found new things to worry about. How could he know if he had faith? He decided the only proof would be a miracle. Walking between Elstow and Bedford, he was about to tell the puddles in the road to dry up and the dry places to become puddles. Then he thought he had better pray first. Then he thought: if I pray and it still doesn't work, that will prove I have no faith at all. So he didn't try.

Around this time he had a kind of dream. He saw the Bedford people sitting on the sunny side of a mountain, while he shivered in the snow outside a wall. At last he found a tiny gap and squeezed through, head first, then his shoulders, then the rest of him, and sat down with them in the sun. He understood the wall as God's word and the gap as Jesus, the way to the Father, and the gap was narrow for a reason: “here was only room for body and soul, but not for body and soul, and sin.”

Look at the difference between the puddles and the mountain. The puddle test was Bunyan trying to prove himself to himself. The gap in the wall was God showing him that the way in is a person, Jesus, and that you can't drag your old life through with you. And look at what drew him in the first place: not an argument, but ordinary people whose faith was so real that joy made them talk.

One thing to do this week: find one person whose faith seems real and joyful to you, someone who talks about God like those women in the sun. Ask them one honest question this week: how did God first become real to you?

study_questions.question: What did the women in Bedford talk about that Bunyan had never thought of?
study_questions.answer: The new birth, God's work in their hearts, his love to them in Jesus, and how useless their own goodness was. They spoke as if joy made them speak.

study_questions.question: Why didn't Bunyan try the puddle “miracle”?
study_questions.answer: He was afraid that if he prayed and it failed, it would prove he had no faith at all, so he never tried.

study_questions.question: What did the narrow gap in the wall stand for?
study_questions.answer: Jesus Christ, the way to God. It was so narrow that there was room for body and soul but not for body, soul and sin.

One day his work took him to Bedford, and in one of the streets he came across “three or four poor women sitting at a door in the sun, and talking about the things of God.” By now he thought of himself as a bit of an expert on religion, so he drew near to listen. “I heard, but I understood not.” They weren't talking about rules. “Their talk was about a new birth, the work of God on their hearts.” They talked about how God had shown them his love in Jesus, about the promises that had comforted them, and about their own unbelief and how useless their own goodness was. And they talked like happy people: “methought they spake as if joy did make them speak.” To Bunyan it was as if they had found a new world. His heart began to shake. He realised he had never once thought about a new birth. He went back to his work, but their conversation went with him, and he kept finding excuses to go back and listen again. He noticed two new things inside himself: a soft, tender heart, and a mind that wouldn't stop thinking about God. His mind, he says, hung on to it “like a horse leech at the vein.” Not everyone he knew was going the same way. He had a close friend named Harry, a hard swearer, whom he now stopped spending time with. When they met in a lane and Bunyan asked him why he swore like that and what would happen to him if he died, Harry snapped back, “What would the devil do for company, if it were not for such as I am?” The poor man who had first got Bunyan reading the Bible joined a group called the Ranters, who taught that people who had reached their kind of perfection couldn't sin whatever they did. Bunyan, unsure what was true, prayed one of the most sensible prayers in the book: “O Lord, I am a fool, and not able to know the truth from error: Lord, leave me not to my own blindness.” But his anxious mind found new things to worry about. How could he know if he had faith? He decided the only proof would be a miracle. Walking between Elstow and Bedford, he was about to tell the puddles in the road to dry up and the dry places to become puddles. Then he thought he had better pray first. Then he thought: if I pray and it still doesn't work, that will prove I have no faith at all. So he didn't try. Around this time he had a kind of dream. He saw the Bedford people sitting on the sunny side of a mountain, while he shivered in the snow outside a wall. One thing to do this week: find one person whose faith seems real and joyful to you, someone who talks about God like those women in the sun. Ask them one honest question this week: how did God first become real to you?

fields.title: And Yet There Is Room
fields.body_html:
“And the servant said, Lord, it is done as thou hast commanded, and yet there is room.” — Luke 14:22 (KJV)

You might think Bunyan was nearly there. Instead, two new fears grabbed him. The first was: “Whether I was elected?” In other words, had God chosen him at all? He read in Romans that salvation “is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy,” and it seemed to trample on everything he wanted. The tempter, as he calls it, put it simply: “It may be you are not.” And if not, “you had as good leave off, and strive no further.”

For weeks he walked around so weighed down that he felt he might sink where he stood. Then one day a sentence came into his mind with great comfort: “Look at the generations of old and see; did ever any trust in the Lord, and was confounded?” He went home sure he would find it in the Bible straight away. He couldn't. He asked his friends, and they couldn't either. It took him more than a year to find it, and when he did, it was in Ecclesiasticus, one of the books called the Apocrypha, which Protestants don't count as part of the Bible.

That rattled him at first. But by then he had learned more of God's kindness, and he reasoned that the sentence was “the sum and substance of many of the promises.” The Bible really is full of people who trusted God and were not let down. “I bless God for that word, for it was of God to me.”

Then came the second fear: what if the day of grace was over? What if he had left it too late? He imagined that the good people of Bedford were all the people God was going to save in that area, and that they had got the blessing before he arrived. He walked around kicking himself: “Oh, that I had turned sooner! Oh, that I had turned seven years ago!”

He was so worn out he could hardly take another step when, near the same spot as before, these words from Jesus' story of the great feast broke into his mind: “Compel them to come in, that my house may be filled,” and “and yet there is room.” Those last words, he says, “were sweet words to me.” There was room in heaven for him. He even believed that when Jesus first told that story, he was already thinking of people like Bunyan, who would one day be afraid there was no space left.

He still longed to be sure that Christ had called him. Reading about Jesus calling his disciples, he wished, “Would I had been in their clothes; would I had been born Peter; would I had been born John.” For months he heard nothing. But he kept asking.

Notice the shape of both fears. “What if I'm not one of the chosen ones?” and “What if I'm too late?” are really the same fear: what if there's no place for me? It's the feeling of walking into a party where everyone already has a group, and the good seats are gone. Bunyan's answer came straight from the mouth of Jesus. Whatever else is true, the host of this feast is still sending out invitations, and his servant's report is “yet there is room.”

One thing to do this week: read Jesus' story of the great supper in Luke 14:15-24. Notice who ends up at the table. Then write the words “and yet there is room” somewhere you'll see them every day this week.

fields.title: Thou Art My Love
fields.body_html:
“For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Romans 8:38-39 (KJV)

At last Bunyan started telling the Bedford Christians how he was feeling. They told their pastor, John Gifford, who invited Bunyan to his house to listen to him talking with others about how God works in people's lives. And then something unexpected happened. The closer Bunyan got, the worse he felt.

He began to notice what was going on inside him, the wrong thoughts and desires he had never paid attention to before. His heart felt cold and dragging, “as a clog on the leg of a bird to hinder her from flying.” He was sure he was going backwards. “I was more loathsome in my own eyes than was a toad,” he wrote, and sin seemed to bubble out of his heart “as water would bubble out of a fountain.” He was convinced “that everyone had a better heart than I had.” He even envied animals, because “they had not a sinful nature.” This went on, he says, “even for some years together.”

Friends tried to point him to God's promises. It was no use: “they had as good have told me that I must reach the sun with my finger.” But he did one wise thing. He did not want to get rid of his guilt the wrong way, by distracting himself or just waiting for the feeling to fade. He had seen people do that and come out harder than before. He wanted his guilt dealt with properly, by Christ.

The turn came through a sermon on two words from the Song of Songs, “My love.” The preacher said that even when a believer is tempted and feels deserted by God, they are still Christ's love. Bunyan “got nothing” from it at the time. But walking home, he thought, “What shall I get by thinking on these two words?” And the words began to burn: “Thou art my love, thou art my love,” twenty times over, louder and warmer. He kept answering, “But is it true, but is it true?” Then the voice inside him grew stronger still, adding that nothing would separate him from that love.

He was so full of joy that he said he could have told the crows sitting on the ploughed fields about God's mercy, if they could have understood him. He wished he had pen and ink to write it down there and then, “for surely I will not forget this forty years hence; but alas! within less than forty days, I began to question all again.”

That last sentence is one of the most honest in the book. Real experiences of God's love do not always stay bright. They fade, and the doubts come back. That doesn't mean the first experience was fake.

And look at “everyone had a better heart than I had.” Almost everyone feels this, because you see the whole messy inside of your own head and only the outside of everyone else. Getting closer to God often makes you more aware of what's wrong, not less, and that can be a sign of life rather than proof you're failing. But if a heavy, hopeless feeling about yourself sits on you for weeks and won't lift, it's not just a spiritual problem to battle alone. Talk to a parent, a pastor, or a doctor. Low mood like that is common, and real help exists.

One thing to do this week: write down one moment when God's love felt real to you, with the date, the way Bunyan wished he had pen and ink. Keep it somewhere safe. On the days the feeling has gone, read it again.

study_questions.answer: “My love.” On the way home they kept repeating in his mind, “Thou art my love,” until his heart was full of comfort and hope.

study_questions.answer: Within forty days he began to doubt it all again. His honesty shows that faded feelings do not mean the experience of God's love was fake.

fields.title: Floods of Blasphemies
fields.body_html:
“And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.” — Luke 22:31-32 (KJV)

A week or two later, a Bible verse began to follow Bunyan around: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you.” Once it sounded so loudly that he turned his head, sure someone half a mile behind him was calling his name. Looking back, he believed it was a warning that a storm was coming.

It came about a month later, and he says it “handled me twenty times worse than all I had met with before.” First his comfort went. Then darkness. Then “whole floods of blasphemies, both against God, Christ, and the Scriptures, were poured upon my spirit.” Was there really a God? Was the Bible just a clever story? Muslims had their scriptures too; “how if all our faith, and Christ, and Scriptures, should be but a think-so too?” Thoughts like these filled his mind from morning to night.

Then it got worse. Whenever he heard people talk about the sin against the Holy Spirit, which Jesus says will never be forgiven, he felt a terrible pull to commit it, as if his mouth would say the words whether he wanted to or not. “Often I have been ready to clap my hand under my chin, to hold my mouth from opening.” At times he even thought of throwing himself head first into a hole in a dung heap, just to stop his mouth speaking. When he tried to pray, his mind would flash pictures at him, “a bush, a bull, a besom” (a broom), as if he should pray to those instead. He could hardly cry. He thought he was possessed, or going mad, and he was sure that nobody who loved God could ever have thoughts like his.

But in the middle of it all he noticed one thing. “Only by the distaste that they gave unto my spirit, I felt there was something in me that refused to embrace them.” The thoughts horrified him. He hated them. That hatred was the real Bunyan.

This lasted about a year. Then, slowly, God brought him out. Walking in the country one day, he remembered that Christ “made peace through the blood of his cross,” and saw “that God and my soul were friends by this blood.” Pastor Gifford taught him not to take any truth second-hand but to ask God to make it real to him from the Bible. And he found an old book, Martin Luther's commentary on Galatians, so old it was falling apart, and it described his own experience “as if his book had been written out of my heart.”

Let's be really clear here, because this chapter may be about you. Many people, including many sincere Christians, get sudden, unwanted, horrible thoughts that pop up out of nowhere, often about the very things they care about most: God, the people they love, their own safety. It is very common. Some modern writers have wondered whether Bunyan had what doctors now call OCD; no one can diagnose a man who died in 1688, but his description will sound familiar to many people today. Here is what Bunyan found, and what doctors would tell you too: a thought you hate is not a thought you chose. It is not who you are. Fighting it harder usually makes it louder, and hiding it makes it heavier. Bunyan felt completely alone; you don't have to be. Talk to a pastor, and also to a doctor or counsellor, because people who understand this can genuinely help. And if thoughts of hurting yourself ever come with them, tell a safe person straight away: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live.

One thing to do this week: if you have been carrying thoughts like Bunyan's, tell one safe adult this week, a parent, pastor, teacher, doctor or counsellor. You don't have to say the thoughts out loud in detail; “I keep getting horrible thoughts I don't want” is enough to start. If that's not you, pray for someone who might be fighting this silently.

study_questions.question: What kinds of thoughts attacked Bunyan during this year?
study_questions.answer: Floods of blasphemous thoughts and doubts about whether God existed and whether the Bible was true, along with a terrible pull to say words against the Holy Spirit that he did not want to say.

study_questions.question: What clue did Bunyan notice that the thoughts were not really his own desires?
study_questions.answer: He saw that the thoughts disgusted him. Something in him “refused to embrace them,” and that showed where his heart really was.

study_questions.question: What should someone do if they have unwanted thoughts like these?
study_questions.answer: Not hide them or fight them alone, but talk to a pastor and to a doctor or counsellor, and tell a safe person at once if thoughts of self-harm come too.

fields.title: Let Him Go, If He Will
fields.body_html:
“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — 1 John 1:7 (KJV)

For a while Bunyan had real peace. He loved Christ, he says, “as hot as fire.” Then the worst temptation of his life arrived. It was a single thought: sell Christ. Swap him for the things of this life, for anything at all.

It came for a whole year, often every hour. He couldn't eat, pick up a pin, chop a stick, or look at anything without the thought joining in: “Sell Christ for this, or sell Christ for that; sell Him, sell Him.” Sometimes it ran a hundred times in a row. He fought it with everything he had. He would push with his hands and elbows, answering out loud as fast as the thought came, “I will not, I will not, I will not, I will not; no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands of worlds.”

Sometimes the temptation even dressed itself up as holiness. In the middle of a meal it would insist that he must stop eating and go and pray immediately, or he would displease God. If he finished his food, he then felt as guilty as if he'd disobeyed God himself.

Then one morning, lying in bed, the thought came again, “as fast as a man could speak.” He answered, “No, no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands, at least twenty times together.” He was almost out of breath. And then this thought passed through his heart: “Let Him go, if He will!” He felt as if his heart had agreed.

“Now was the battle won, and down I fell, as a bird that is shot from the top of a tree, into great guilt, and fearful despair.” He got out of bed and wandered into a field, where for two hours he was “like a man bereft of life.” A verse from Hebrews landed on him about Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal: “he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.” Bunyan was sure that was him now. “Nothing now for two years together would abide with me, but damnation, and an expectation of damnation.”

There were small breaks in the cloud. Walking by a hedge, months later, the words came to him, “The blood of Christ remits all guilt,” and then, “The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” For a moment he saw that his sin, compared with the blood of Christ, was like “this little clot or stone before me” compared with “this vast and wide field.” The peace lasted two or three hours. Then the verse about Esau came back.

Look closely at what happened that morning. A man who loved Christ was hammered with one unwanted thought, hundreds of times a day, for a year. He fought it until he was exhausted, and then one tired, panicked thought slipped through. Was that really the same as choosing to reject Jesus? In the chapters ahead, Bunyan himself comes to see that it was not.

If your mind ever gets locked into a loop like this, where you argue and argue with a thought and it only gets stronger, please hear this: that is not a sign that you are wicked or that God has left you. It is a pattern many people's minds fall into, and it is known and treatable. Bunyan had to fight it almost alone for years. You don't. Talk to someone you trust, and let a pastor and a doctor or counsellor help you carry it. If the despair ever turns into thoughts of hurting yourself, tell a safe person straight away.

One thing to do this week: if you are stuck in a mental argument you can't win, stop trying to win it on your own. Tell one person you trust what is going on. Saying it out loud to someone safe is not giving in; it is getting help.

study_questions.question: What was the temptation that followed Bunyan for a year?
study_questions.answer: The constant thought “sell Christ,” trading him for anything at all, which came into his mind with almost everything he did.

study_questions.question: What happened one morning in bed?
study_questions.answer: After answering “No” at least twenty times, he was exhausted, and the thought “Let Him go, if He will!” passed through his heart. He felt he had agreed to it and fell into despair.

study_questions.question: Why might that moment not be the same as really rejecting Jesus?
study_questions.answer: He had fought the thought for a year with all his strength; it was one tired thought that slipped through against his will, not a calm decision. Bunyan himself later saw the difference.

In the middle of a meal it would insist that he must stop eating and go and pray immediately, or he would displease God. If he finished his food, he then felt as guilty as if he'd disobeyed God himself. Then one morning, lying in bed, the thought came again, “as fast as a man could speak.” He answered, “No, no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands, at least twenty times together.” He was almost out of breath. And then this thought passed through his heart: “Let Him go, if He will!” He felt as if his heart had agreed. “Now was the battle won, and down I fell, as a bird that is shot from the top of a tree, into great guilt, and fearful despair.” He got out of bed and wandered into a field, where for two hours he was “like a man bereft of life.” A verse from Hebrews landed on him about Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal: “he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.” Bunyan was sure that was him now. “Nothing now for two years together would abide with me, but damnation, and an expectation of damnation.” There were small breaks in the cloud. Walking by a hedge, months later, the words came to him, “The blood of Christ remits all guilt,” and then, “The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” For a moment he saw that his sin, compared with the blood of Christ, was like “this little clot or stone before me” compared with “this vast and wide field.” The peace lasted two or three hours. Then the verse about Esau came back. Look closely at what happened that morning. A man who loved Christ was hammered with one unwanted thought, hundreds of times a day, for a year. He fought it until he was exhausted, and then one tired, panicked thought slipped through. Was that really the same as choosing to reject Jesus? In the chapters ahead, Bunyan himself comes to see that it was not. If your mind ever gets locked into a loop like this, where you argue and argue with a thought and it only gets stronger, please hear this: that is not a sign that you are wicked or that God has left you. It is a pattern many people's minds fall into, and it is known and treatable. Bunyan had to fight it almost alone for years. You don't. Talk to someone you trust, and let a pastor and a doctor or counsellor help you carry it. If the despair ever turns into thoughts of hurting yourself, tell a safe person straight away. One thing to do this week: if you are stuck in a mental argument you can't win, stop trying to win it on your own. Tell one person you trust what is going on. Saying it out loud to someone safe is not giving in; it is getting help.

fields.title: Weary of My Life
fields.body_html:
“Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more? Is his mercy clean gone for ever? doth his promise fail for evermore? Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies?” — Psalm 77:7-9 (KJV)

Bunyan now believed he had committed the one sin that could never be forgiven. He searched the Bible for anyone who had done what he had done. King David committed adultery and murder, but Bunyan decided David had sinned against the law, while he had sinned against the Saviour himself. Peter denied Jesus three times, which came closest, but Peter had only denied his master; Bunyan thought he had sold his. “Wherefore I thought with myself, that I came nearer to Judas, than either to David or Peter.”

He tried comparing his sin with Judas's too, looking for any difference, “though but the breadth of an hair.” He found some: Judas acted on purpose, after thinking it through, while Bunyan's thought came “in a fearful hurry, on a sudden,” against everything he was praying for. That helped for a little while, and then the fear came back.

In this chapter of his life Bunyan wrote one of the saddest sentences in the book: “And now was I both a burden and a terror to myself, nor did I ever so know, as now, what it was to be weary of my life, and yet afraid to die.” He wished he could be anybody but himself.

He read the story of Francis Spira, an Italian lawyer from the century before who had turned back from his faith and died in despair. It was, Bunyan said, like “salt, when rubbed into a fresh wound.” His body shook for days at a time. He felt such pressure in his chest that it seemed his breastbone would split.

He dreaded praying, because he thought God had shut him out. The tempter told him prayer would only make things worse. In the end he decided: “I can but die; and if it must be so, it shall once be said, that such an one died at the foot of Christ in prayer.” So he prayed, though it was very hard.

Then he did something brave and told an older Christian the whole story, including his fear that he had sinned against the Holy Spirit. The man “told me he thought so too.” Cold comfort, Bunyan says. Talking longer, he realised the man was good but did not understand this kind of struggle. So Bunyan did not give up; he went back to God.

One day he walked to a nearby town and sat down on a bench in the street, thinking about where his sin had brought him. When he finally looked up, it seemed to him that the sun was unwilling to give him light, and that the very stones in the street and the tiles on the roofs were against him, as if the whole world wanted him gone.

There are three things to take from this, and the first matters most. If you have ever felt “weary of my life, and yet afraid to die,” you are not the first, and it does not mean God has given up on you. Please tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live. Second, if the first person you tell gets it wrong, as that old man did, don't stop there. Tell someone else. Third, Bunyan later wrote that the root of all these fears was “my being misinformed of the nature of my sin.” His terror was real. His conclusion was wrong. That can be true for you too.

One thing to do this week: if you have been feeling weary of life or have had thoughts of not wanting to be here, tell one safe person this week, and if you ever feel in danger, contact a crisis line where you live right away. If that's not where you are, learn the crisis number for your country and save it in your phone, so you have it ready for yourself or a friend.

fields.title: My Grace Is Sufficient for Thee
fields.body_html:
“And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (KJV)

Still sitting on that bench, Bunyan burst out, “How can God comfort such a wretch as I?” And straight away, “as an echo doth answer a voice,” came the words, “This sin is not unto death.” He felt “as if I had been raised out of a grave.” If his sin was not the sin unto death, then it could be forgiven. For the first time he felt he stood “upon the same ground with other sinners.”

It didn't last long. The next evening, afraid again, he prayed, “O Lord, I beseech thee, show me that thou hast loved me with everlasting love.” The answer came back like an echo: “I have loved thee with an everlasting love.” He went to bed at peace and woke up believing it. Over the next days the message grew clearer: “I loved thee whilst thou wast committing this sin, I loved thee before, I love thee still, and I will love thee for ever.”

But the struggle wasn't over. It would be “well-nigh two years and an half” before he was really free. Oddly, he found comfort even in that. “Many days are not for ever, many days will have an end.”

One day the tempter told him there was no point praying. Here is Bunyan's account, and it is worth reading slowly: “Yet, thought I, I will pray. But, said the tempter, your sin is unpardonable. Well, said I, I will pray. It is to no boot, said he. Yet, said I, I will pray.” So he prayed: “Lord, Satan tells me that neither Thy mercy, nor Christ's blood, is sufficient to save my soul; Lord, shall I honour Thee most, by believing Thou wilt and canst? or him, by believing Thou neither wilt nor canst? Lord, I would fain honour Thee, by believing Thou wilt and canst.”

Then one morning in prayer, part of a verse broke in: “My grace is sufficient.” Only two weeks before, he had read that very verse, thought it “not large enough for me,” and thrown the book down in a temper. Now it seemed to have “arms of grace so wide that it could not only enclose me, but many more besides.” But he noticed something was missing: the words “for thee.” So he asked God for those too.

Some time later, sitting in a meeting full of fear, he heard it whole: “My grace is sufficient for thee, my grace is sufficient for thee, my grace is sufficient for thee,” three times over. Every word felt huge. It was “as though I had seen the Lord Jesus look down from heaven through the tiles upon me.”

For weeks after, his mind was like a pair of scales: on one side the verse about Esau, on the other “My grace is sufficient,” and his peace went up and down “sometimes twenty times a day.” Finally he asked God to let both verses hit him at once, to see which would win. A few days later they did. The verse about Esau grew weak and faded, and grace won.

Another verse became his favourite of all: “And him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” The tempter told him Christ meant other, better sinners, not him. Bunyan answered: “Satan, here is in this word no such exception; but 'him that comes', him, any him.” He describes fighting for that verse like a tug-of-war: “he pulled and I pulled; but, God be praised, I got the better of him.”

If you are in the up-and-down stage, Bunyan's story says that's not failure. Healing for him was not one bright moment but a scale tipping back and forth for weeks before it settled. And notice what he held on to. Not his feelings, but the words: “for thee,” and “him, any him.”

One thing to do this week: pick one of Bunyan's two verses, “My grace is sufficient for thee” or “him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out,” and learn it by heart this week. When a doubt comes, answer it the way Bunyan answered the tempter: yet I will pray.

study_questions.answer: “This sin is not unto death,” which came to him like an echo as he sat on the bench in the street.

study_questions.answer: Because the words “for thee” were missing, and he wanted to know the promise was for him personally. Later he heard the whole phrase three times over.

study_questions.question: How did Bunyan answer when Satan said John 6:37 was not meant for him?
study_questions.answer: He said there was no exception in the verse: “him that comes,” meaning any him, including himself.

fields.title: Thy Righteousness Is in Heaven
fields.body_html:
“But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” — 1 Corinthians 1:30 (KJV)

Bunyan found a picture that helped him in an old law of Moses. Someone who killed another person by accident, without hating them, could run to a “city of refuge” and be protected there. Bunyan saw himself in that law. He had not hated Christ; he had loved him, prayed to him, and fought that wicked thought for a whole year. So “I thought verily I was the man that must enter, because I had smitten my neighbour unwittingly, and hated him not aforetime.”

Then he did something he had been too scared to do for years. He went back and actually read, carefully, the frightening verses in Hebrews that had haunted him. “I found their visage changed; for they looked not so grimly on me as before I thought they did.” Hebrews 6 was about people who fall away completely and openly, rejecting Christ in front of the world. Esau had not had a sudden panicked thought; he made a calm, public choice and went on despising his birthright for years. That was not Bunyan's story.

Then one day, walking through a field, still a bit uneasy, he heard a sentence in his soul: “Thy righteousness is in heaven.” He seemed to see Jesus Christ at God's right hand. That was where his righteousness was, his rightness with God. And he saw something that changed everything: “it was not my good frame of heart that made my righteousness better, nor yet my bad frame that made my righteousness worse; for my righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself, the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever.”

“Now did my chains fall off my legs indeed.” He went home rejoicing. When he looked for the sentence in the Bible and couldn't find it, his heart began to sink again, until he remembered that Christ “of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.” The truth was there after all.

He gives a lovely picture of what this meant. The good things growing in him were like the small cracked coins a rich man carries in his pocket, while his real wealth is locked away safe at home. “Oh, I saw my gold was in my trunk at home! In Christ, my Lord and Saviour!”

Looking back, Bunyan thought he could see two causes of his long trial. One was that after his first deliverance he had only prayed to be rescued from present troubles, and never asked God to guard him from future ones. “I do beseech thee, reader, that thou learn to beware of my negligence.” The other was that once, during his first wife's painful pregnancy, he had secretly tested God, asking him to stop her pains that night as proof that God knew his thoughts. She fell asleep peacefully. Later he felt he should have simply trusted God rather than put an “if” on him.

He came out with a deep sense of how big grace is. “Great sins to draw out great grace.” He would still have hard times; once, when he was seriously ill and afraid to die, the words “justified freely by his grace” turned his fear into joy. But the worst was over.

Here is the heart of this chapter. Your standing with God does not rise and fall with your mood. On your best day, your rightness with God is Christ. On your worst day, it is still Christ. And when a Bible verse frightens you, don't run from it and don't obsess over it alone. Read it in context, with someone wise. Bunyan found the verses he feared most “looked not so grimly” when he finally faced them properly.

One thing to do this week: write 1 Corinthians 1:30 on a card or in your phone. On a day when you feel far from God, read it and say: my righteousness is not my mood today; it is Christ.

study_questions.answer: That his rightness with God was Jesus Christ himself at God's right hand, so his good or bad moods could not make it better or worse.

study_questions.answer: Kept praying for God to protect him from temptations still to come, not just to rescue him from present trouble.

fields.title: In Chains to Them in Chains
fields.body_html:
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.” — 1 Corinthians 13:1 (KJV)

About five or six years after his struggles began, some of the most respected members of the Bedford church asked Bunyan to speak at one of their meetings. He was shaken by the idea, but he agreed, and spoke twice in private. They were moved and thanked God. After prayer and fasting, the church set him apart to preach in public. “When the country understood, they came in to hear the Word by hundreds.”

He could hardly believe God was using him. “I at first could not believe that God should speak by me to the heart of any man.” But people kept telling him he had shown them the way to Christ, and in the end he had to accept it.

He preached exactly what he had lived through. For the first two years he preached about sin and guilt, because that was what he was still feeling. “I preached what I felt, what I smartingly did feel.” Then he wrote one of the most famous lines in the book: “I went myself in chains to preach to them in chains; and carried that fire in my own conscience that I persuaded them to beware of.” Sometimes he walked up to the pulpit full of guilt and terror, felt free while he was preaching, and was “as bad as I was before” before he got to the bottom of the stairs. Later, as God gave him more peace, he preached about Christ, and then about being joined to Christ.

He loved the people who came to faith. When any of them later fell away, he said it hurt him more “than if one of my own children, begotten of my body, had been going to its grave.” He wanted to go to the darkest places, to people who had never heard. And he was still tempted while he preached: by blasphemous thoughts, by sudden blankness, “as if my head had been in a bag,” and by pride.

Against pride, he used Paul's picture of the cymbal. A cymbal can make wonderful music, but the music comes from the player, not from the cymbal. Gifts are like that. “What, thought I, shall I be proud because I am a sounding brass? Is it so much to be a fiddle?” His conclusion is one of the best things he ever wrote: “great grace and small gifts are better than great gifts and no grace.”

Then came the rumours. People said he was “a witch, a Jesuit, a highwayman.” Worst of all, they said he had lovers and children by them, and even two wives at once. Bunyan denied it all flatly and invited anyone to prove otherwise. He did not chase every rumour down. “I bind these lies and slanders to me as an ornament,” he wrote, remembering Jesus' words about being blessed when people falsely say all kinds of evil against you for his sake.

Notice that Bunyan didn't wait until he was fixed before God used him. He was still fighting fears when he first preached, and he says so. God used his broken places to reach broken people. And notice his warning about gifts. Being talented, popular or a good speaker is not the same as being close to God. A little grace, he said, “a little love, a little of the true fear of God, is better than all these gifts.”

One thing to do this week: think of one gift you have, anything from music to listening to fixing things. This week, use it once quietly for someone else's good, and when you're done, thank God for it instead of waiting for anyone to praise you.

study_questions.question: What did the cymbal picture teach him?
study_questions.answer: That gifts can make beautiful “music” for God and still be lifeless in themselves. Great grace with small gifts is better than great gifts and no grace.

He preached exactly what he had lived through. For the first two years he preached about sin and guilt, because that was what he was still feeling. “I preached what I felt, what I smartingly did feel.” Then he wrote one of the most famous lines in the book: “I went myself in chains to preach to them in chains; and carried that fire in my own conscience that I persuaded them to beware of.” Sometimes he walked up to the pulpit full of guilt and terror, felt free while he was preaching, and was “as bad as I was before” before he got to the bottom of the stairs. Later, as God gave him more peace, he preached about Christ, and then about being joined to Christ. He loved the people who came to faith. When any of them later fell away, he said it hurt him more “than if one of my own children, begotten of my body, had been going to its grave.” He wanted to go to the darkest places, to people who had never heard. And he was still tempted while he preached: by blasphemous thoughts, by sudden blankness, “as if my head had been in a bag,” and by pride. Against pride, he used Paul's picture of the cymbal. A cymbal can make wonderful music, but the music comes from the player, not from the cymbal. Gifts are like that. “What, thought I, shall I be proud because I am a sounding brass? Is it so much to be a fiddle?” His conclusion is one of the best things he ever wrote: “great grace and small gifts are better than great gifts and no grace.” Then came the rumours. People said he was “a witch, a Jesuit, a highwayman.” Worst of all, they said he had lovers and children by them, and even two wives at once. Bunyan denied it all flatly and invited anyone to prove otherwise. He did not chase every rumour down. “I bind these lies and slanders to me as an ornament,” he wrote, remembering Jesus' words about being blessed when people falsely say all kinds of evil against you for his sake. Notice that Bunyan didn't wait until he was fixed before God used him. He was still fighting fears when he first preached, and he says so. God used his broken places to reach broken people. And notice his warning about gifts. Being talented, popular or a good speaker is not the same as being close to God. A little grace, he said, “a little love, a little of the true fear of God, is better than all these gifts.” One thing to do this week: think of one gift you have, anything from music to listening to fixing things. This week, use it once quietly for someone else's good, and when you're done, thank God for it instead of waiting for anyone to praise you.

fields.title: Leap off the Ladder
fields.body_html:
“But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound” — Romans 5:20 (KJV)

In those years England had brought back the king, and new laws said worship had to follow the Church of England. Preachers like Bunyan who would not stop holding their own meetings could be arrested. In November 1660, after about five years of preaching, Bunyan was arrested at a meeting of believers in the countryside before he could preach. He was charged with holding “unlawful assemblies and conventicles,” meaning illegal religious meetings. He could have gone free if he promised not to preach. He would not. So he went to Bedford gaol, and he stayed there for twelve years.

By then his first wife had died, and he had married again; his second wife, Elizabeth, was left at home with four children, the eldest his daughter Mary, who had been born blind. Bunyan does not soften what this cost. “The parting with my wife and poor children hath often been to me in this place as the pulling the flesh from the bones.” Above all he worried about “my poor blind child, who lay nearer my heart than all beside.”

Listen to him: “Poor child! thought I, what sorrow art thou like to have for thy portion in this world! Thou must be beaten, must beg, suffer hunger, cold, nakedness, and a thousand calamities, though I cannot now endure the wind should blow upon thee.” He felt “as a man who was pulling down his house upon the head of his wife and children; yet thought I, I must do it, I must do it.” He believed God would care for them if he stood firm. But he never pretends it was easy, or that his family did not pay for his choice. They did.

Early on, not knowing the law, he feared he might be hanged. For weeks he felt nothing of God at all, and he was afraid that if he climbed the gallows ladder he would shake and go pale, and shame the gospel. Then he settled it. God could choose whether to comfort him; Bunyan's job was to stand firm. “If God doth not come in, thought I, I will leap off the ladder even blindfold into eternity, sink or swim, come heaven, come hell, Lord Jesus, if thou wilt catch me, do; if not, I will venture for thy name.” He remembered how Satan had sneered that Job only served God for what he got out of it, and decided that serving God even with nothing in return was the sign of an honest heart.

Prison also gave him the closest time with God of his whole life. “I never had in all my life so great an inlet into the Word of God as now.” It was there that he wrote this book, and years later came The Pilgrim's Progress, which tells the same journey as a story. He was released in 1672, and died in 1688.

He ends with honesty, not a victory lap. He still finds “seven abominations” in his heart, starting with “Inclinings to unbelief.” Sometimes a single line of the Bible was more than he could take in; other times “the whole Bible hath been to me as dry as a stick.” But he had learned where to run. “Of all tears, they are the best that are made by the blood of Christ.”

Bunyan's story doesn't end with a man who never doubts again. It ends with a man who knows that his hold on God was never the thing keeping him safe. God's hold on him was. Faith, in the end, looked like jumping blindfold, trusting Christ to catch him, with or without the feelings.

One thing to do this week: write a short honest prayer in Bunyan's style: “Lord Jesus, if thou wilt catch me, do.” Then name one thing you are afraid of, and one person (like Bunyan's Mary) you want to trust God with. Pray it every day this week.

study_questions.question: Why was Bunyan put in prison, and for how long?
study_questions.answer: He was arrested in 1660 for preaching at meetings outside the Church of England and refused to promise to stop preaching. He stayed in Bedford gaol for twelve years.

study_questions.question: How did he feel about leaving his family, especially his blind daughter?
study_questions.answer: It felt like “pulling the flesh from the bones.” He feared terribly for his blind child, who lay “nearer my heart than all beside,” and he admits his choice was like pulling his house down on his family.

study_questions.question: What did Bunyan mean by leaping “off the ladder even blindfold into eternity”?
study_questions.answer: That even if he felt no comfort from God, he would stay faithful and trust himself to Christ, asking Jesus to catch him.
